newsitem.title: FINLAND: Clinton braced for tough talks with Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Clinton braced for tough talks with Yeltsin.

text.p: A wheelchair-bound U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday prepared for potentially sticky talks with Russian President Boris Yeltsin over NATO's plan to expand east into the Kremlin's old sphere of influence.

Clinton and Yeltsin, who was bouncing back into the global spotlight after being sidelined for more than six months because of heart surgery and pneumonia, arrived within hours of each other for their first summit in nearly a year.
The U.S. president, wheeled off his aircraft and on to a catering truck that lowered him to the airport tarmac, spent his final hours before meeting Yeltsin huddled with his advisers.

The run-up to the Clinton-Yeltsin meeting brought a torrent of tough talk about NATO expansion from the Russians, with Yeltsin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky warning that Russia might forge closer, competing ties with China, India and Iran.
But Yeltsin took a softer line on his arrival in Helsinki, telling reporters compromise was possible.
Clinton responded in kind.
"I was quite encouraged," Clinton told reporters when asked how he viewed Yeltsin's remarks. "I felt good about it. I'm looking forward to it (the summit)."

The two leaders were to start their first meeting since each won re-election last year, and the 11th meeting of their presidencies, with a dinner hosted by Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari on Thursday evening.

Before the dinner, at the Helsinki presidential palace where U.S. President George Bush and Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev held crisis talks in 1990 before the Gulf War with Iraq, Clinton met Ahtisaari to discuss bilateral issues.
The important business of the summit was to take place on Friday at Ahtisaari's secluded official residence.

Clinton, temporarily in a wheelchair after knee surgery due to a freak accident that delayed the summit by one day, hopes to persuade a hostile Yeltsin that NATO plans for enlargement are no threat to Russia and will enhance European security.
An alliance summit in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to be the first former east-bloc nations to start membership talks.
U.S. officials have been adamant that NATO enlargement will go forward despite protests by Russia, which feels that the alliance's enlargement is a threat to its security.
"I don't expect them to change their views and they shouldn't expect us to change our views," National Security Adviser Sandy Berger told reporters.
In addition to the future shape of NATO -- and Russia's relationship with it -- Clinton and Yeltsin were to discuss arms control and Russia's transformation to a market economy.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry sought to play down expectations, saying many matters were still unresolved.
"There's a lot of very difficult work that lies ahead and some differences that will be difficult to bridge," he said.

A key U.S. arms control aim was to win a Russian pledge to ratify by this spring the START-2 strategic arms reduction treaty, which would reduce U.S. and Russian arsenals of nuclear warheads to 3,500 warheads each, a senior U.S. official said.
Another U.S. official said that on the economic front, Clinton would press for significant changes in Russian legal and tax treatment of commercial properties and investments.
The U.S. president was prepared to offer "a package of incentives for U.S. investors to respond to those changes".
The Clinton administration has asked Congress to provide $900 million in aid to Russia and the newly independent states of Eastern Europe this year, up from $614 million last year.
Clinton told reporters that his knee injury had not proved an impediment to his work on the summit.
"So far we're doing all right," he said. "My knee and I are getting around pretty well."
